#

library(mirt)
library(psych)
library(psychTools)
data(bfi)
names(bfi)
 scores <- psych::scoreItems(bfi.keys,bfi,min=1,max=6)
 scores

items<-subset(bfi, select=c(A1,A2,A3,A4,A5,C1,C2,C3,C4,C5,
E1,E2,E3,
E4,E5,N1,N2,N3,N4,N5,O1,O2,O3,O4,O5))

items_t<-wt*t(items)
items_t<-wt*t(items)

                   F3=E1,E2,E3,E4,E5
                   F4=N1,N2,N3,N4,N5

messages.subject: Re: Testlet model
messages.subject_clean: Testlet model
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

in 'specific' you specify which item belongs to which testlet (i.e., dimension). Rep is a function in base R that simply repeats a given number a specified number of times. a1, a2, a3, and a4 are the item slopes for each dimension. You got three dimensions in total: a general one and three specific ones for the testlets.
In COV you specify the variances and covariances of your dimensions. In your case the specific factors are not allowed to correlate, since only variances but no covariances are specified.

Best

messages.subject: bfactor: factor score estimation method, effects on item residual correlations
messages.subject_clean: bfactor: factor score estimation method, effects on item residual correlations
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

the scenario is as follows:

1. I am sampling from a bifactor (testlet) model using simdata().
2. I fit a unidimensional model. Item residual correlations within testlets are greater zero, whereas between testlets they are close to zero. Thus, there is a violation of local stochastic independence caused by the testlets, as expected.
3. To account for item residual correlations within testlets, I fit a bifactor model using bfactor(). Expectation: All item residual correlations should be near zero.
4. Item residual correlations are estimated with Q3 and thus require the estimation of factor scores/person parameters.
5. Estimation with MAP leads to negative item residual correlations within testlets, whereas correlations between testlets remain largely unaffected. However, when using EAP estimates for person parameters from the bifactor model (with Quasi-Monte-Carlo-Integration), item residual correlations behave as expected, with all of them being close to zero.

This occurs both at very high dimensionality (> 40 testlets) and lower levels of dimensionality (10 testlets).

My questions are as follows:

1. Why do EAP and MAP estimates lead to such a different outcome here?
2. What is the recommened estimation method for person parameters after fitting a model with bfactor()? Does the dimension-reduction EM algorithm reduce dimensionality in such a way that EAP estimates are warranted and may actually yield more accurate results?

Thank you very much for your help.

Best

There is no single difficulty parameter in multidimensional models; they represent vectors of locations across the probability space, and therefore there are an infinite number of them (in a 3D surface plot with the 2PLM, think how many possible combinations could result in P(theta1_theta2) = .5, for example)

No, this is a curse of dimensionality. If you're lucky to have some 0 cross-loadings for a given item the itemplot() function has a drop.zeros argument to reduce the dimensionality of a given item, but for the overall test the number of dimensions cannot be reduced without marginalizing information.

>
> Another question - how do you explore the results for more ten 2 or 3 dimensions? It's not graphically reproducable, then what to extract from the results (only coef() function's results?) ? So far for simple models I created my own python script to extract from intercept, slope and guessing all the functions including standard error measure, so I was curious whether I can get those results from mirt directly.

I think you just have to become more comfortable with the mathematical aspects of the models for higher dimensional tests, as you're correct visualization starts to fail. Similar problems happen in all multidimensional modeling methods (e.g., think structural equation modeling and why response surfaces are never visualized in that framework). HTH.

messages.subject_clean: estimation procedures
messages.body_plain:
Hi Sebastian,

Functionally the ideas are the same in that numerical integration is performed using quasi-monte carlo methods. In the mirt() call this grid is used multiple times for integration during the E-step, while in other functions this grid should only be used once (like in itemfit() or M2(), for instance). Rule of thumb though; if you're using stochastic estimation methods, as well as the quasi-monte carlo integration during estimation, then it's usually best to set QMC = TRUE if subsequent function calls as well to improve the numerical integration quality. HTH.

Phil

Hi Briana,

I wouldn't recommend using Fisher's information matrix in this case as it requires integrating across the possible response data space (which can be enormous, even for shorter tests). Methods based on the observed information matrix are likely better for IRT for this very reason, which is why the default is the numerical Oakes method. HTH.

Phil

I don't think such a thing is possible in the mirt() function right now, though you may be able to trick the mixedmirt() syntax into doing this. It would require specifying a latent regression model via lr.fixed, constrain the loadings to apply only to one latent trait, and set the residual variance of the trait to 0 (though not exactly 0, as this won't work in the computations of a density with the VCOV matrix). I'd have to experiment with this myself, though admittedly it is quite ad hoc. You might have better luck doing something like this in a SEM framework using a package like lavaan.

Phil

messages.body_plain:
No, the distribution selected (e.g., Gaussian) serves effectively as a Bayesian prior distribution for the latent trait. As Baysian priors go, they could be wrong and bias the results, though with sufficient information (i.e., number of items/responses) the prior will get overwhelmed by the likelihood component and asymptotically becomes irrelevant. For finite test lengths, and particularly shorter tests, selection of an incorrect latent trait distribution can have negative consequences (this is true of all latent variable models, not just those in IRT).

Phil
